---
title: "Waste materials and leachate chemistry exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Sum the reactions

Combine the two pyrite/iron stages and show the final oxygen and water coefficients.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Add equations and cancel Fe²⁺.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
FeS₂ + **15/4 O₂ + 7/2 H₂O** → Fe(OH)₃ + 2 SO₄²⁻ + 4 H⁺. Fe, S, O, H, and charge balance. The product charge is −4 + 4 = 0.
:::

## 2. A shortfall

The worked pyrite inventory reacts fully, but only 0.0150 mol accessible CaCO₃ is available. Calculate the residual acid equivalents for the stated endpoint.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Subtract two equivalents per mole of accessible calcite from the generated amount.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Acid generated = 0.0400 mol eq; neutralised = 0.0300 mol eq; residual = **0.0100 mol eq**. Final pH still requires a water volume and the remaining acid–base equilibria.
:::

## 3. Concentration versus load

Discharge A is 10.0 L/s with dissolved Fe 2.00 mg/L. Discharge B is 40.0 L/s with Fe 1.00 mg/L. Which exports more iron?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Multiply each concentration by its own flow.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
A exports **20.0 mg/s**, B **40.0 mg/s**. B has lower concentration but twice the load. These are dissolved loads and do not include suspended iron solids.
:::

## 4. Long-term claim

A treated waste initially gives neutral-pH water. What evidence is needed before concluding that future metal and acid release will stay low?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Consider remaining reactive inventories, access, rate, and stability.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Check remaining sulfide and neutralising minerals, oxygen/water access, weathering rates, pH/redox changes, flow, dissolved/solid inventories, and relevant-duration leach observations. One initial pH does not establish long-term stability.
:::

## Explore: acid potential versus neutralisation {#explore}

Predict what happens to a heap that drains at neutral pH today if the same
calcite can neutralise only one equivalent per mole instead of two. Does the
acid potential change, or only how long the drainage stays neutral? Change one
input at a time.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="acidbase" role="group" aria-label="Acid potential versus neutralisation in mine waste">
<p>Reference case: one tonne of waste with 1 % pyrite has an acid potential of 333 eq H⁺. With 7.5 kg reachable CaCO₃ at the CO₂* endpoint (150 eq) and an oxidation rate of 0.02 per year, the calcite is used up after about 30 years and 183 eq of acid remain to drain out.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/acidbase.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Worked example**. Check the acid potential, the CaCO₃ needed
and the year the calcite runs out by hand. Then double the oxidation rate.
Which numbers change, and which stay fixed?

**E2.** Compare **Near-neutral endpoint** and **Half the calcite coated**. Why
do they give the same curves although the reasons are chemically different?

**E3.** Choose **Calcite-rich heap**, then lower the reachable share of calcite
until the drainage eventually turns acidic. Explain why a neutral leachate
alone could not tell this heap apart from the worked example.

### Model conditions and hand check

The constructed case is one tonne of waste with 1.0 % FeS₂ by mass:
`10 000 g / 120 g/mol = 83.3 mol FeS₂`. At 4 H⁺ per FeS₂ the acid potential is
**333 eq/t**, with 167 mol sulfate. Neutralising it needs 333 / 2 = 167 mol
CaCO₃ = **16.7 kg/t** at the CO₂\* endpoint, or 33.3 kg/t at the near-neutral
endpoint. The waste holds 7.5 kg/t CaCO₃ = 75 mol, worth **150 eq/t** at the
CO₂\* endpoint. Cumulative acid generated is `333 × (1 − e^(−0.02 t))`; it
reaches 150 eq when `t = −ln(1 − 150/333) / 0.02 ≈ 30 years`. After all pyrite
has reacted, **333 − 150 = 183 eq/t** of acid remain.

Assumptions: pyrite oxidises completely to sulfate and Fe(OH)₃ (4 H⁺ per
FeS₂), at a first-order rate chosen for illustration only. Calcite is the only
neutraliser, and the reachable part reacts as fast as acid forms until it is
used up; the rest never reacts. Each mole of CaCO₃ neutralises 2 eq (CO₂\*
endpoint) or 1 eq (near-neutral, HCO₃⁻ stays in solution). Rates of calcite
dissolution, oxygen supply, flow paths, other minerals and dilution are
omitted. The curves are amounts per tonne, not concentrations or pH.
